'''''Euonymus europaeus''''', the '''spindle''', '''European spindle''', or '''common spindle''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Celastraceae]], [[native plant|native]] to much of Europe, where it inhabits the edges of forest, hedges and gentle slopes, tending to thrive on nutrient-rich, chalky and salt-poor soils. It is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]].

==Description==
''Euonymus europaeus'' grows to {{convert|3|-|6|m|0|abbr=on}} tall, rarely {{convert|10|m|0|abbr=on}}, with a stem up to {{convert|20|cm|0|abbr=on}} in diameter. The [[leaf|leaves]] are opposite, [[lanceolate]] to elliptical, 3–8 cm long and 1–3 cm broad, with a finely serrated edge.<ref name = "Dirr1998" /> The base is cuneate.<ref name="Thomas_et_al2011">{{cite journal |last1=Thomas |first1=Peter A |last2=El-Barghathi |first2=M |last3=Polwart |first3=A |title=Biological Flora of the British Isles: Euonymus europaeus L. |journal=Journal of Ecology |date=2011 |volume=99 |pages=345–365 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2745.2010.01760.x }}</ref> Leaves are dark green in summer. Autumn colour ranges from yellow-green to reddish-purple, depending on environmental conditions.<ref name = "Dirr1998">Dirr, Michael A. 1998. Manual of Woody Landscape Plants, 5th ed</ref>

The [[plant sexuality|hermaphrodite]] [[flower]]s are produced in late spring and are insect-pollinated. They are rather inconspicuous and small with yellowish-green petals, and grow in [[inflorescence|cymes]] of 3–8 together. The capsular [[fruit]] ripens in autumn, and is red to purple or pink in colour and approximately 1–1.5 cm wide. When ripe, the four lobes split open to reveal the orange [[seed]]s.

==Habitat and ecology==

''E. europaeus'' occurs as an understorey shrub or small tree primarily in old hedgerows, open woodland clearings and margins, and scrubland on base-rich or calcareous soils. However, it is also shade-tolerant. It rarely invades open habitats such as grasslands unless abundant hedges are present<ref name= "Thomas">{{cite journal | doi=10.1111/j.1365-2745.2010.01760.x | title=Biological Flora of the British Isles: ''Euonymus europaeus'' L. | date=2011 | last1=Thomas | first1=Peter A. | last2=El-Barghathi | first2=M. | last3=Polwart | first3=A. | journal=Journal of Ecology | volume=99 | issue=1 | pages=345–365 | s2cid=86183760|doi-access=free | bibcode=2011JEcol..99..345T }}</ref> In Ireland, it can also be found growing on rocky limestone outcrops, rocky lake shores and [[limestone pavement]]s.<ref>Green P. 2008. Flora of County Waterford. National Botanic Gardens of Ireland, Dublin, Ireland.</ref>

It is typical in ''[[Fraxinus excelsior]]'' – ''[[Acer campestre]]'' – ''[[Mercurialis perennis]]'' [[British NVC community W8|woodland (W8)]], and it is a frequent companion of ''[[Cornus sanguinea]]'' in open-stand scrub over [[limestone]], generally in low frequency and abundance throughout.<ref>Rodwell JS. 1991. ''British Plant Communities. Vol. 1''. Woodlands and Scrub. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK</ref> Its distribution is usually scattered, but it may occasionally occur remarkably commonly on a local scale. An example of this is in the so-called "Spindle Valley" in the [[Chilterns]].<ref>Snow B, Snow D. 1988. ''Birds and Berries''. Poyser, Calton, UK.</ref> The scattered distribution is likely limited by dispersal of seeds via birds and rodents.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.2307/2960555 | jstor=2960555 | title=Interaction of Irradiance and Soil Nutrient Supply on Growth of Seedlings of Ten European Tall-Shrub Species and ''Fagus Sylvatica'' | last1=Grubb | first1=Peter J. | last2=Lee | first2=William G. | last3=Kollmann | first3=Johannes | last4=Wilson | first4=J. Bastow | journal=Journal of Ecology | date=1996 | volume=84 | issue=6 | pages=827–840 | bibcode=1996JEcol..84..827G }}</ref>

''E. europaeus'' is the almost exclusive winter host of the [[black bean aphid]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.2307/2403294
 | jstor=2403294 | title=The Distribution and Abundance of the Spindle Tree, ''Euonymus europaeus'', in Southern England with Particular Reference to Forecasting Infestations of the Black Bean Aphid, ''Aphis fabae'' | last1=Way | first1=M. J. | last2=Cammell | first2=M. E. | journal=Journal of Applied Ecology | date=1982 | volume=19 | issue=3 | pages=929–940 | bibcode=1982JApEc..19..929W }}</ref> Because of the potential economic loss from this insect that feeds on cultivated [[broad bean]]s and [[sugar beet]], spindle in the past was commonly removed from hedges and woodlands as a measure against black bean aphid outbreaks and agricultural yield losses, although this widespread removal does not appear to have impacted current populations. In 1944, The Biology War Committee also began a campaign to investigate the distribution and ecology of ''E. europeaus'' as a basis for aphid control measures.<ref name= "Thomas"/>

==Cultivation and uses==
 
It is a popular [[ornamental plant]] in gardens and parks due to its bright pink or purple fruits and attractive autumn colouring.

In cultivation in the UK, the [[cultivar]] 'Red Cascade' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=''Euonymus europaeus'' 'Red Cascade' AGM|url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/99750/Euonymus-europaeus-Red-Cascade/Details |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=23 June 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 37 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 20 February 2018}}</ref>

European spindle wood is very hard, and can be cut to a sharp point. In the past it was used to make [[spindle (textiles)|spindles]] for spinning wool and for butchers' skewers.<ref>Clapham, A. R. (1975). ''The Oxford Book of Trees''. Oxford: Oxford University Press. p.31.</ref>

[[Charcoal (art)|Charcoal]] produced from this plant is held in high esteem among artists for its exceptional strength and density.

Parts of the plant have been used for medicinal purposes.<ref>[[Plants for a Future]]: [http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Euonymus+europaeus ''Euonymus europaeus'']</ref> However, the fruit is poisonous and contains several toxic substances, including the [[alkaloid]]s [[theobromine]] and [[caffeine]], as well as a large number of much more toxic substances, including [[cardiac glycoside]]s, and an extremely bitter [[terpene]]. Poisoning is more common in young children, who are attracted to the brightly coloured fruits. Ingesting them can result in liver and kidney damage, or even death.<ref>{{cite web  | url=https://www.fathen.org/beware-the-poisonous-autumn-berries/| title = Beware the poisonous autumn berries! | date = October 2011 | publisher = Fat Hen The Wild Cookery School | access-date = 15 September 2020}}</ref>
